messages.subject_clean: outflank Fst vs uncorrected Fst odd results
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
this is more of a theoretical question about Outflank.

I hope you can provide your feedback or experience.

I know that the Uncorrected Fst (used by Outflank) should be similar to the corrected Fst, so they should lie on the middle line when plotting them against each other.
This would mean that the the sample is not so different across loci (I think).

However, in my case I have 2 lines of loci one shifted slightly higher than the other...I am assuming it means that a group of loci has different (I think higher ?) sample size than the other group of loci...now how much of a problem is this in Outflank?

In the Whitlock paper (2015), I read that "For datasets that have unequal sample sizes among populations but no missing data (i.e., all loci are equally unbalanced), the inference of outliers from our procedure will not be affected. However, for datasets that have large differences in per-population sample size among loci(perhaps due to sequencing errors or differences in coverage), inference on loci with different sampling properties than the rest of the dataset should be interpreted with caution and confirmed with re-sequencing".

In my case, I don't seem to  have different coverage/call rate of loci per population (as assessed through gl.report.callrate by locus), so does it mean I should not worry about this?

Plot attached.
I would appreciate any feedback!
Thank you!
Best,
Gabriella

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have converted my genlight dataset into .lfmm for use with the pcadapt package (outliers detection). Everything seems to be ok, but when I run pcadapt and I get the number of outliers, I only get a list of indexes, not the names of the loci.

Is there a way to get the actual outlier loci names?
Or at least to know if in the .lfmm file  they are listed in the same order as in the genlight file?

This issue seems to have been reported before -->
https://groups.google.com/g/dartr/c/oQBefOgCCg0/m/sww0EYoaAAAJ
So I wonder if it was ever solved?

Below my code:
I converted my genlight file to geno (.lfmm) with gl2geno (dartR2.7.2) and then reading the file with read.pcadapt

<
my.dataset_PCAdapt_file_gl2geno = read.pcadapt(
    "C:/Users/scatag/my.dataset_geno_dev.lfmm",
    type = c("pcadapt"),
    type.out = c("matrix"),
    allele.sep = c("/"))

my.dataset_PCAdapt_file_gl2geno_PCADAPTres <- pcadapt(
    input =  my.dataset_PCAdapt_file_gl2geno ,
    K = 50)

qval <- qvalue(
     my.dataset_PCAdapt_file_gl2geno_PCADAPTres$pvalues)$qvalues

alpha <- 0.1

  outliers_my.dataset_PCAdapt_file_gl2geno <- which(qval < alpha)
  length(outliers_my.dataset_PCAdapt_file_gl2geno) # 96

outliers_my.dataset_PCAdapt_file_gl2geno  #  4  431  759  939 1035 1401 ....
>

It gives me only the index of the outliers, not the name...

I would love some feedback and advice on how to proceed.

Also, anyone would recommend other outlier detection methods? Outflank detects 0 outliers and pcadapt 96 outliers in the same dataset, so I am unsure of which would be more correct. It would be interesting to try a different method and see what the results of the 3rd method are closest to.

Thank you for your help!
Best
Gabriella

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabriella,

If you use the "bed" format from plink, as shown in the code below, the order of the loci is the same as in the results of pcadapt.

library(pcadapt)
library(dartR)
gl2plink(testset.gl <http://testset.gl>,
         plink_path = getwd(),
         bed_file = TRUE,
         outpath = getwd(),
         outfile = "test")
filename <- read.pcadapt("test.bed", type = "bed")
x <- pcadapt(filename, K = 3)
padj <- p.adjust(x$pvalues,method="bonferroni")
alpha <- 0.1
outliers <- locNames(testset.gl <http://testset.gl>)[which(padj < alpha)]

You could try also redundancy analysis: https://doi.org/10.1111/mec.14584

Cheers,
Luis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Oumar,

If you have a genlight object already, presumably produced by DArT, you may find that it does not include a trimmedsequence field in the locus metadata. DArT have only recently been generating this as  routine.

So you would have a couple of options. 1. Ask DArT to regenerate your report with trimmed sequences included; or 2. Trim 6 bp off the end of the Sequences. You will lose a bit of data this way, because not all of the sequence will have adaptor residues.

Then use gl2fasta to generate your fastA file.

See how that goes. ☺️

messages.body_plain:
Hi Renee,

Something like this:

# installing developing version of dartR
devtools::install_github("green-striped-gecko/dartR@dev")
library(dartR)
# reading vcf
t1 <- gl.read.vcf(system.file('extdata', 'test.vcf', package = 'dartR'))
# SNP nucleotides
t1$loc.all
# removing loci that are not SNPs
# this filtering is performed within the function but include here just for
# testing purposes
no_SNP <- which(nchar(t...@loc.all) >3 )
t1 <- gl.drop.loc(t1,loc.list = locNames(t1)[no_SNP])
t1 <- gl.filter.monomorphs(t1)

t2 <- t1[,1:10]
as.matrix(t2)
t...@loc.all

# method 4: the heterozygous state is resolved by randomly assigning one or
# the other SNP variant to the individual.
gl2fasta(t1,
         method = 4,
         trimmed.sequence = FALSE,
         outfile = "output.fasta",
         outpath = getwd())

system(
"./iqtree2  -s output.fasta -m GTR+ASC"
)

# ERROR: For your convenience alignment with variable sites printed to output.fasta.varsites.phy
# ERROR: Invalid use of +ASC because of 19 invariant sites in the alignment

system(
  "./iqtree2  -s output.fasta.varsites.phy -m GTR+ASC"
)

Cheers,
Luis

Hi Renee and others,

DartR was initially designed to take reports from Diversity Arrays Technology (DArT), which would include trimmed sequences if requested as part of the service. We have expanded capability to include a wider range of data sources, including vcf files. We are pretty happy to continue to expand this capability, but it is likely that we will compartmentalize this as follows.

gl.read.vcf ...... gl.compliance.check ...... [dartR gl.object] ..... gl2fasta ..... [desired fastA file]

If you have generated the sequence tags outside of DArT, or if you do not have trimmed sequences (easy fix in this case is to copy AlleleSequence to TrimmedSequence), and you are happy with a fastA file that only contains the state change at the SNP locus, then I guess it is possible to modify gl2fasta to take the SNP transitions from gl@other$loc.metrics$SNP rather than from the sequence tags.

This is if I have my head around the problem. I am not familiar with the stacks pipeline and the content of a genlight object brought in from a vcf file. If you clarify, we can give this mod a shot.

A

messages.subject: Re: Interpreting kinship estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Naomi,

Yes, the kinship estimates from the snpgdsIBDMLE() function use the same scale as the gl.grm() function in dartR.

Two alleles are identical by descent (IBD) if they are identical copies of the same ancestral allele in a base population. Relatedness is the proportion of alleles shared between individuals that are IBD. Kinship is the probability that two alleles, one taken at random from each individual, are IBD (Wang, 2022). Kinship considers half the genetic information because it looks at the probability that one individual inherits a particular allele from a common ancestor shared with another individual. Therefore, kinship is equal to half of relatedness.

Wang, J. (2022). A joint likelihood estimator of relatedness and allele frequencies from a small sample of individuals. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 13(11), 2443-2462.
Cheers,
Luis

I suspect the problem comes from the name of your individuals. Please read the documentation of the function (see below) by typing in the R console: ?gl.run.structure

popNames(gl) <- gsub(" ","_",popNames(gl))

indNames(gl) <- gsub(" ","_",indNames(gl))

It's also worth noting that Structure truncates individual names at 11 characters. The function will fail if the names of individuals are not unique after truncation. To avoid this possible problem, a number sequence, as shown in the code below, might be used instead of individual names. indNames(gl) <- as.character(1:length(indNames(gl)))

Cheers,
Luis

Hi,

Here is some code to get you started. You can also read our tutorials: dartR -- R Package for SNP analysis | Georges Lab (biomatix.org) <http://georges.biomatix.org/dartR>

library(dartR)
t1 <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
# Table of chromosomes
tbl_chrom <- table(t1$other$loc.metrics$Chrom_Platypus_Chrom_NCBIv1)
# getting chromosomes with at least 50 SNPs
list_chrom <- names(tbl_chrom)[which(tbl_chrom > 50)]
#list to store genlight objects by chromosome
chrom_list <- as.list(1:length(list_chrom))
for(i in 1:length(list_chrom)){
  # getting the index of snps for each chromosome
  tmp <- which(t1$other$loc.metrics$Chrom_Platypus_Chrom_NCBIv1 == list_chrom[i])
  # subsetting the snps by chromosome
  chrom_list[[i]] <- gl.keep.loc(t1,loc.list = locNames(t1)[tmp])
}
# naming each genlight object using chromosomes
names(chrom_list) <- list_chrom

#for each chromosome
# Number of SNPs
chrom_snps <- lapply(chrom_list, nLoc)
# chromosome size:
# https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCA_900231445.1/
# SNP density
for(i in 1:length(chrom_list)){

  chr_tmp <- chrom_list[[i]]
  # setting chromosome name
  chr_tmp$chromosome <- chr_tmp$other$loc.metrics$Chrom_Platypus_Chrom_NCBIv1
  # setting SNP position
  chr_tmp$position <- chr_tmp$other$loc.metrics$ChromPos_Platypus_Chrom_NCBIv1

  ggplot(data.frame(snp=chr_tmp$position),aes(x=snp)) +
    geom_rug(length = unit(0.05, "npc")) +
    labs(title=unique(as.character(chr_tmp$chromosome)))

}

#transitions, and transversions
lapply(chrom_list, gl.report.bases)
#MAF
lapply(chrom_list, gl.report.maf)
#PIC
lapply(chrom_list,gl.report.locmetric,metric = "AvgPIC" )

Cheers,
Luis
